primary_sources: House Committee on Un-American Activities, hearings on the movie industry, 1947

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the HUAC hearings on the movie industry, 1947

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the House Committee on Un-American Activities hearings on the movie industry, 1947. Paraphrased, not quoted, because the source is after 1929.
stimulus.text: In 1947, the House Committee on Un-American Activities held hearings on communism in the movie industry. The committee called writers and directors to testify about their politics and to name others with communist ties. Ten witnesses, later called the Hollywood Ten, refused to answer the committee's questions, citing their First Amendment rights. They were jailed for contempt of Congress, and studio heads agreed not to hire anyone suspected of communist ties.

stem: The blacklist that followed the hearings worked by

options.text: Courts convicting actors of espionage in public trials.
options.misconception: No actors were tried for espionage over the hearings. The blacklist was enforced by employers, not by courts or trials.

options.text: Congress passing a law that banned all films about communism.
options.misconception: Congress passed no law banning films. The blacklist was an agreement among studio heads, not a statute.

options.text: Audiences boycotting movie theaters across the country.
options.misconception: The blacklist came from studio heads, not from audiences.

options.text: Studios refusing to hire people accused of communist ties.

rationales.A: Background: no actors were tried for espionage over the hearings. The blacklist was enforced by employers, not by courts or trials.
rationales.B: Background: Congress passed no law banning films. The blacklist was an agreement among studio heads, not a statute.
rationales.C: Background: audiences did not organize the blacklist. Studio heads drew it up to show their patriotism and protect their business.
rationales.D: Background from the books: eager to show patriotism, the heads of the major studios set up a blacklist of people suspected of communist ties, and the accused could find no work.
rationales.general:
1. After the hearings, the heads of the major studios agreed not to hire anyone suspected of communist ties.
2. A person on the list could find no work in Hollywood, even without any trial or conviction.
3. The punishment therefore came from private employers, not from a court or a law.
Remember: A blacklist punishes by denying work, and private employers can enforce it without any law.
